subject: Database Management Systems
title: DBMS UNIT - I: Master Revision Deck (30 Cards)

cards.front: What is the complete visual roadmap and core architecture of DBMS Unit 1?
cards.back: DBMS Unit 1 guides you through six major building blocks: (1) Database Fundamentals (what databases are and how engines work), (2) Conceptual Database Design (drawing real-world ideas as ER diagrams), (3) Advanced ER and EER (handling special categories and child entities), (4) Relational Data Model (turning ideas into clean tables with safety rules), (5) Logical Database Design (the 7-step recipe to convert diagrams into SQL tables), and (6) Relational Querying and Views (finding information with queries and creating custom viewing windows).
cards.key_takeaway: Unit 1 moves step-by-step from real-world ideas to diagrams, tables, safety rules, and searches.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  T1["Topic 1: Fundamentals"] --> T2["Topic 2: Conceptual ER"]
  T2 --> T3["Topic 3: Advanced EER"]
  T3 --> T4["Topic 4: Relational Model"]
  T4 --> T5["Topic 5: Schema Mapping"]
  T5 --> T6["Topic 6: Queries & Views"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Overview

cards.front: What is the textbook definition of a Database and a DBMS?
cards.back: A database is a collection of interrelated data and a set of programs to access those data. A database-management system (DBMS) consists of a collection of interrelated data and a set of programs to access those data. The primary goal of a DBMS is to provide a way to store and retrieve database information that is both convenient and efficient.
cards.key_takeaway: A database is the organized collection of facts; a DBMS is the safe software engine that lets us access and search it.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph LR
  Data["Interrelated Data (Facts)"] --> Engine["DBMS Software Engine"]
  Engine --> User["Convenient & Efficient Access"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 1: Database Fundamentals -> 1.1 Definition

cards.front: Why do traditional file systems fail compared to a modern DBMS?
cards.back: Old-fashioned file systems store information in separate text files, which causes seven big headaches: data redundancy (the same address is saved in five different places), data inconsistency (updating one file leaves old data in another), difficulty in finding facts (requiring a programmer to write a new script for simple questions), data isolation, lack of security, data integrity errors, and crash failures where half-written records corrupt the whole system.
cards.key_takeaway: File systems scatter duplicate data without safety rules; a DBMS centralizes data with strict integrity and crash recovery.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  Old["Old File Systems: Scattered Files | Duplication | Crashes"] -->|Replaced By| DBMS["Modern DBMS: One Central Store | Safe Rules | Automatic Backups"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 1: Database Fundamentals -> 1.2 File System Drawbacks

cards.front: What are the three levels of Data Abstraction in the ANSI/SPARC architecture?
cards.back: The database hides complicated hard drive details across three levels: (1) Physical Level (how data is physically saved on the disk as bits and blocks), (2) Logical Level (what tables and columns exist and the rules that connect them), and (3) View Level (the personalized window each individual person sees, hiding secret columns like teacher salaries from student screens).
cards.key_takeaway: Physical describes HOW data is stored on disk; Logical describes WHAT tables exist; View describes WHO is allowed to see what.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  V["View Level (Custom Windows for Users)"] --> L["Logical Level (Tables, Columns & Rules)"]
  L --> P["Physical Level (Hard Drive Bits & Blocks)"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 1: Database Fundamentals -> 1.3 Data Abstraction

cards.front: What happens during Conceptual Database Design?
cards.back: Conceptual Database Design is the creative phase where software engineers talk to clients (like college deans or hospital managers), find out what real-world things exist (like Students, Courses, and Teachers), and draw an Entity-Relationship (ER) diagram. This phase focuses entirely on business meaning and relationships without worrying about which database software (like MySQL or Oracle) will be used later.
cards.key_takeaway: Conceptual design turns real-world business requirements into a clear visual ER blueprint independent of computer hardware.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph LR
  Req["Client Requirements"] --> Analyze["Identify Entities & Links"] --> ER["Conceptual ER Diagram"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 2: Conceptual Design -> 2.1 Overview

cards.front: What are the standard geometric shapes used in an ER diagram?
cards.back: In Chen's standard ER notation: (1) Rectangles represent Strong Entity Types (like `Student`), (2) Double Rectangles represent Weak Entity Types (like `Dependent`), (3) Diamonds represent Relationship Types (like `Enrolls_In`), (4) Ovals represent Attributes (like `Name`), (5) Underlined Ovals represent Primary Keys (like `Roll_No`), (6) Double Ovals represent Multi-valued Attributes (like `Phone_Numbers`), and (7) Double Lines represent Total Participation (mandatory involvement).
cards.key_takeaway: Rectangles are entities, diamonds are relationships, ovals are attributes, and double lines show mandatory participation.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  Rect["Rectangle: Entity"] --- Diam["Diamond: Relationship"]
  Oval["Oval: Attribute"] --- UndOval["Underlined Oval: Key"]
  DblOval["Double Oval: Multi-Valued"] --- DblRect["Double Rectangle: Weak Entity"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 2: Conceptual Design -> 2.2 ER Core Constructs

cards.front: What is the Extended Entity-Relationship (EER) model, and what new tools does it add?
cards.back: The Extended Entity-Relationship (EER) model adds advanced object-oriented features to basic ER diagrams. It allows us to group similar things together using Superclasses and Subclasses (like a general `Employee` parent with specialized `Doctor` and `Nurse` children). Children automatically inherit all attributes from their parent (Attribute Inheritance), preventing us from redrawing the same columns over and over again.
cards.key_takeaway: EER adds inheritance and parent-child hierarchies (IS-A relationships) so subclasses automatically share superclass attributes.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  Parent["Superclass: PERSON (Name, ID)"] -->|Inherits| Child1["Subclass: STUDENT (GPA)"]
  Parent -->|Inherits| Child2["Subclass: TEACHER (Salary)"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 3: Extended ER -> 3.1 Foundations

cards.front: What is the Relational Model, and how does it organize information?
cards.back: The Relational Model represents all database information in simple, clean two-dimensional tables called Relations. In this model: (1) Every table has a unique name, (2) Each row represents a single real-world record called a Tuple, (3) Each column represents a property called an Attribute, and (4) Strict Integrity Rules ensure that rows can always be uniquely identified and connected without missing pointers.
cards.key_takeaway: The relational model stores all data in tables (relations) of rows (tuples) and columns (attributes) protected by integrity rules.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph LR
  Table["Table (Relation)"] --> Rows["Rows (Tuples: Records)"]
  Table --> Cols["Columns (Attributes: Properties)"]
  Table --> Rules["Integrity Rules (Keys & Types)"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 4: Relational Model -> 4.1 Foundations

cards.front: What is the 7-Step ER-to-Relational Mapping Recipe?
cards.back: To convert an ER diagram into real database tables, engineers follow a 7-step algorithm: (Step 1) Create a table for each regular entity, (Step 2) Create a table for weak entities embedding the parent's key, (Step 3) Map 1:1 relationships using foreign keys, (Step 4) Map 1:N relationships by putting the 1-side key into the N-side table, (Step 5) Map M:N relationships by creating a new bridge table, (Step 6) Put multi-valued attributes into their own separate tables, and (Step 7) Map n-ary relationships into multi-key join tables.
cards.key_takeaway: The 7-step mapping algorithm is the standard formula that converts visual ER diagrams into normalized relational tables.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  S1["1. Regular Entities"] --> S2["2. Weak Entities"]
  S2 --> S3["3. 1:1 Links"]
  S3 --> S4["4. 1:N Links"]
  S4 --> S5["5. M:N Tables"]
  S5 --> S6["6. Multi-Valued Attributes"]
  S6 --> S7["7. N-ary Relations"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 5: Logical Design -> 5.1 Algorithm

cards.front: What are Relational Queries, Views, and Schema Evolution?
cards.back: After tables are built, users interact with them in three ways: (1) Querying: Asking questions using declarative SQL (`SELECT`) to retrieve answers instantaneously; (2) Views: Creating virtual glass windows that show specific rows and columns while hiding private data; and (3) Schema Evolution: Adding or altering table columns over time (`ALTER TABLE`) without having to delete existing data or shut down the database.
cards.key_takeaway: Queries search data, views create safe custom viewing windows, and schema evolution updates table structures over time without data loss.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  Usage["Using the Database"] --> Q["1. Queries: Search Data"]
  Usage --> V["2. Views: Safe Custom Windows"]
  Usage --> E["3. Evolution: Alter Tables Without Loss"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 6: Relational Querying -> 6.1 Overview

cards.front: What are the four functional sub-languages of SQL, and what does each perform?
cards.back: SQL is partitioned into four functional sub-languages: (1) DDL (Data Definition Language) to define and modify schema objects (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE); (2) DML (Data Manipulation Language) to query and mutate relation tuples (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE); (3) DCL (Data Control Language) to administer privileges and permissions (GRANT, REVOKE); and (4) TCL (Transaction Control Language) to manage atomic transaction boundaries (COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT).
cards.key_takeaway: DDL defines structural blueprints; DML modifies tuple instances; DCL enforces security privileges; TCL controls transaction boundaries.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  SQL["SQL Grammar"] --> DDL["DDL: Structure (CREATE, ALTER)"]
  SQL --> DML["DML: Data (SELECT, INSERT)"]
  SQL --> DCL["DCL: Security (GRANT, REVOKE)"]
  SQL --> TCL["TCL: Transactions (COMMIT, ROLLBACK)"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 1: Database Fundamentals -> 1.5 Database Languages

cards.front: What are the six engineering phases of the Database Lifecycle in sequential order?
cards.back: The six engineering phases are: (1) Requirements Analysis (gathering stakeholder needs and compiling the Software Requirements Specification), (2) Conceptual Database Design (producing an ER/EER schema independent of DBMS software), (3) Logical Database Design (mapping ER constructs into normalized relational schemas), (4) Schema Refinement / Normalization (evaluating functional dependencies to eliminate update anomalies), (5) Physical Database Design (selecting file organizations, B+-tree indexes, and clustering), and (6) Security & Implementation (provisioning user roles, access control, and testing).
cards.key_takeaway: Database engineering proceeds systematically: Requirements -> Conceptual ER -> Logical Relational -> Normalization -> Physical Storage -> Deployment.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  P1["1. Requirements Analysis"] --> P2["2. Conceptual ER Design"]
  P2 --> P3["3. Logical Schema Mapping"]
  P3 --> P4["4. Schema Normalization"]
  P4 --> P5["5. Physical Indexing"]
  P5 --> P6["6. Security & Deployment"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 2: Conceptual Design -> 2.1 Lifecycle

cards.front: How are attributes classified into Simple vs Composite, Single-valued vs Multi-valued, and Stored vs Derived?
cards.back: Attributes are classified along three orthogonal engineering axes: (1) Simple attributes are atomic and indivisible (e.g., Salary), whereas Composite attributes decompose into independent components (e.g., Address -> Street, City, Zip); (2) Single-valued attributes contain exactly one atomic scalar per entity (e.g., SSN), whereas Multi-valued attributes hold a set of values (e.g., Skill_Set, Phone_Numbers); (3) Stored attributes are physically written to database pages (e.g., Date_Of_Birth), whereas Derived attributes are dynamically computed on demand (e.g., Age = CURRENT_DATE - Date_Of_Birth).
cards.key_takeaway: Composite attributes decompose into parts; multi-valued attributes hold sets; derived attributes compute values dynamically.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  Attr["Attribute Classifications"] --> Comp["Composite (Address) vs Simple (Age)"]
  Attr --> Multi["Multi-valued (Phones) vs Single-valued (SSN)"]
  Attr --> Deriv["Derived (Age) vs Stored (DOB)"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 2: Conceptual Design -> 2.3 Attributes

cards.front: What are Cardinality Ratios (1:1, 1:N, M:N) and how do they govern relationship structure?
cards.back: The Cardinality Ratio specifies the maximum number of relationship instances in which an entity can participate: (1) One-to-One (1:1): Each entity in set A associates with at most one entity in set B (e.g., Department Manages Manager); (2) One-to-Many (1:N): Each entity in set A associates with any number of entities in set B, but each entity in B associates with at most one entity in A (e.g., Department Employs Employee); (3) Many-to-Many (M:N): Entities in both sets can associate with arbitrary numbers of entities in the opposing set (e.g., Student Enrolls Course).
cards.key_takeaway: Cardinality ratio establishes maximum relationship multiplicity: 1:1, 1:N, or M:N, determining foreign key placement and bridge tables.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  Card["Cardinality Ratios"] --> OneOne["1:1 (Department - Manager)"]
  Card --> OneMany["1:N (Department - Employees)"]
  Card --> ManyMany["M:N (Student - Courses)"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 2: Conceptual Design -> 2.5 Structural Constraints

cards.front: What is the difference between Total Participation (Existence Dependency) and Partial Participation?
cards.back: Participation Constraints specify the minimum number of relationship instances an entity MUST participate in: (1) Total Participation (Existence Dependency) mandates that every entity in the entity set must participate in at least one relationship instance (minimum cardinality >= 1), indicated graphically by a Double Line; (2) Partial Participation allows some entities to exist in the database without participating in the relationship (minimum cardinality = 0), indicated by a Single Line.
cards.key_takeaway: Total participation (double line) enforces mandatory existence (min >= 1); Partial participation (single line) allows optional presence (min = 0).
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph LR
  Total["Total Participation (Double Line: Mandatory)"] === Rel["Relationship"]
  Partial["Partial Participation (Single Line: Optional)"] --- Rel
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 3: Extended ER -> 3.1 Constraints

cards.front: What is a Weak Entity Set, and how is it identified using an owner entity and discriminator?
cards.back: An entity set that does not have sufficient attributes to form a primary key is termed a weak entity set. The entity set on which the weak entity set depends is called the identifying owner or owner entity set. The relationship associating the weak entity set with the identifying owner is called the identifying relationship (represented by a double diamond). A weak entity set possesses a partial key or discriminator (dashed underline), and its primary key is formed by combining the owner's primary key with its own discriminator.
cards.key_takeaway: Weak entity primary key = Owner Primary Key (as foreign key) + Weak Entity Partial Discriminator Key.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph LR
  Owner["Owner: DEPARTMENT (Dept_ID [PK])"] ==>|Identifying Rel| Weak["Weak Entity: DEPENDENT (Dep_Name [Partial])"]
  style Weak stroke-width:3px,stroke-dasharray: 2 2
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 3: Extended ER -> 3.2 Weak Entities

cards.front: What are the formal relational terms for tables, rows, columns, degree, and cardinality?
cards.back: In formal relational model theory: (1) A Table corresponds to a Relation; (2) A Row corresponds to a Tuple; (3) A Column header corresponds to an Attribute; (4) The permitted atomic values for a column correspond to a Domain; (5) The total count of attributes (columns) is the Degree or Arity of the relation; (6) The total count of tuples (rows) is the Cardinality of the relation. Tuples are unordered mathematical sets; no duplicate rows are permitted in a strict relation.
cards.key_takeaway: Table = Relation, Row = Tuple, Column = Attribute, Number of Columns = Degree, Number of Rows = Cardinality.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph LR
  Table["Table (Relation)"] --> Rows["Rows (Tuples) -> Cardinality"]
  Table --> Cols["Columns (Attributes) -> Degree"]
  Cols --> Dom["Domain: Atomic Permitted Values"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 4: Relational Model -> 4.1 Foundations

cards.front: What are the three fundamental Inherent Integrity Constraints of the relational data model?
cards.back: The relational data model enforces three core integrity constraints: (1) Domain Constraints: Every attribute value in every tuple must be an atomic element of that attribute's domain dom(A) or NULL; (2) Entity Integrity Constraint: The entity integrity constraint states that no primary key value can be null; (3) Referential Integrity Constraint: A foreign key in a referencing relation r1 referencing primary key of relation r2 must either match an existing primary key value in r2 or be entirely NULL (preventing dangling pointers).
cards.key_takeaway: Domain enforces atomic types; Entity integrity prohibits NULLs in primary keys; Referential integrity eliminates dangling foreign key references.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  IC["Relational Integrity Constraints"] --> Dom["Domain: Atomic Type Conformity"]
  IC --> Ent["Entity Integrity: Primary Key != NULL"]
  IC --> Ref["Referential Integrity: FK -> Existing PK or NULL"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 4: Relational Model -> 4.3 Integrity Constraints

cards.front: How are Regular Strong Entity Types and Composite Attributes mapped into tables (Step 1)?
cards.back: In Step 1 of ER-to-relational mapping, for each strong entity type E in the ER schema, create a relation R that includes all simple attributes of E. For composite attributes, include only their simple constituent components (flattening the composite hierarchy into distinct scalar columns). Choose one of the candidate keys of E as the primary key of R. Derived attributes are excluded from the physical table schema and computed dynamically via SQL views or generated columns.
cards.key_takeaway: Strong entities map to tables containing simple and flattened composite attributes, designating one candidate key as primary key.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph LR
  Entity["EMPLOYEE (SSN, Name[Fname, Lname], Salary)"] -->|Step 1 Mapping| Table["R_EMPLOYEE(SSN [PK], Fname, Lname, Salary)"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 5: Logical Design -> 5.2 Step 1

cards.front: How are 1:N and M:N Relationship Types mapped into relational tables (Steps 4 & 5)?
cards.back: Mapping rules differ fundamentally based on cardinality: (1) 1:N Binary Relationships (Step 4): Identify the relation representing the entity on the N-side and include as a foreign key the primary key of the relation on the 1-side. (2) M:N Binary Relationships (Step 5): Create a brand new dedicated join/bridge relation R_J. Include as foreign keys in R_J the primary keys of both participating relations; their composite combination forms the primary key of R_J: PK = (PK_S, PK_T). Any descriptive attributes of the M:N relationship are placed inside R_J.
cards.key_takeaway: 1:N embeds the 1-side key as a foreign key on the N-side; M:N creates a separate bridge table with a composite primary key.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  Rel1N["1:N Relationship"] -->|Step 4| Embed["Embed 1-Side PK as FK into N-Side Table"]
  RelMN["M:N Relationship"] -->|Step 5| Bridge["Create Bridge Table with Composite PK (FK1, FK2)"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 5: Logical Design -> 5.5 Steps 4 & 5

cards.front: How do the Storage Manager and Query Processor coordinate during query execution and ACID transaction logging?
cards.back: The Query Processor parses declarative SQL, compiles it into an abstract syntax tree, evaluates heuristic equivalence rewrites (such as selection pushdown), and uses catalog statistics to determine the optimal physical execution plan. During runtime execution, physical operators (IndexScan, HashJoin) request disk pages from the Storage Manager. The Storage Manager's Buffer Pool Manager fetches pages into RAM frames using clock/LRU replacement, the Lock Manager enforces Strict 2PL/MVCC concurrency isolation, and the Recovery Manager logs modifications using Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) to guarantee Atomicity and Durability.
cards.key_takeaway: The Query Processor compiles declarative SQL into an optimal physical plan; the Storage Manager manages RAM frames, locks, and WAL logs.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  QP["Query Processor (Parser -> Optimizer -> Evaluation Engine)"] -->|Requests Pages| SM["Storage Manager (Buffer Pool -> Lock Mgr -> WAL Log Mgr)"]
  SM --> Disk["Physical Disk Blocks (Slotted Pages & Logs)"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 1: Database Fundamentals -> 1.6 Engine Architecture

cards.front: How do Three-Tier enterprise web architectures achieve defense-in-depth security and connection scaling compared to Two-Tier?
cards.back: In Two-Tier Architecture, client workstations execute UI and application logic, establishing direct persistent socket connections (ODBC/JDBC) to the database; this exposes database network ports and exhausts database connection threads. In Three-Tier Architecture, clients execute presentation logic in public tiers (browsers/mobile apps), while business services run on load-balanced application server clusters in an intermediate subnet. The application servers maintain persistent, authenticated database connection pools, multiplexing thousands of client requests across worker threads. The database operates in a private, non-routable subnet, completely eliminating direct client exposure.
cards.key_takeaway: Three-tier architecture pools persistent database connections and isolates the storage engine behind application firewalls.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph LR
  Clients["Ephemeral Clients (Public Web)"] --> AppTier["App Servers (Connection Pools)"]
  AppTier --> DBTier["Database Cluster (Isolated Subnet)"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 1: Database Fundamentals -> 1.7 Client-Server Architecture

cards.front: How do Disjointness (d vs o) and Completeness (Total vs Partial) constraints govern EER Specialization hierarchies?
cards.back: Specialization hierarchies enforce two orthogonal semantic constraints: (1) Disjointness Constraint: Disjoint (d) specifies that subclasses are mutually exclusive, so an entity instance can belong to at most one subclass. Overlapping (o) specifies that an entity may simultaneously belong to multiple subclasses. (2) Completeness Constraint: Total Specialization (double line) mandates that every superclass entity must belong to at least one subclass in the hierarchy. Partial Specialization (single line) allows a superclass entity to exist without belonging to any subclass. The four combinations (Disjoint-Total, Disjoint-Partial, Overlap-Total, Overlap-Partial) define exact subtype membership invariants.
cards.key_takeaway: Disjointness governs overlap (d = mutually exclusive, o = simultaneous); Completeness governs mandatory presence (Total = double line, Partial = single line).
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  Super["Superclass"]
  Super -->|d / o| Circle((d or o))
  Circle --> Sub1["Subclass A"]
  Circle --> Sub2["Subclass B"]
  style Circle fill:#fff,stroke:#333
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 3: Extended ER -> 3.4 Constraints

cards.front: What is Aggregation in the ER model, and why is it necessary to avoid redundant relationship modeling?
cards.back: Aggregation is an abstraction through which relationships are treated as higher-level entities. Classical ER modeling prohibits relationships from directly participating in other relationships. When a relationship must be associated with an external entity (e.g., an Interview relationship between Job_Candidate and Company must be associated with an Evaluation_Report), Aggregation encloses the relationship and participating entities into a composite rectangle, allowing external relationships to connect directly to it without converting the interaction into an ambiguous ternary relationship.
cards.key_takeaway: Aggregation elevates a relationship between entities into a composite higher-level entity that can participate in other relationships.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  subgraph Higher_Entity["Aggregated Entity"]
    E1["Employee"] --- R1["Works_On"] --- P1["Project"]
  end
  Higher_Entity --- R2["Monitored_By"] --- M["Manager"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 3: Extended ER -> 3.6 Aggregation

cards.front: How do ON DELETE CASCADE, SET NULL, and RESTRICT enforce referential integrity during parent deletions?
cards.back: When a referenced primary key tuple in table P is deleted, the DBMS evaluates the declared foreign key referential action: (1) RESTRICT / NO ACTION: The deletion of the parent tuple is aborted immediately if any referencing child rows exist in table C; (2) CASCADE: The deletion automatically cascades, recursively deleting all child rows in table C whose foreign key matches the deleted primary key; (3) SET NULL: All referencing foreign key columns in child tuples in table C are automatically updated to NULL (requiring foreign key columns to be nullable); (4) SET DEFAULT: Referencing foreign key columns in child tuples are reset to their defined default value.
cards.key_takeaway: Referential cascades maintain integrity on parent mutations: RESTRICT aborts, CASCADE propagates deletions, SET NULL nullifies foreign keys.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  ParentDeleted["Parent Primary Key Deleted"] --> Policy{Foreign Key Rule}
  Policy -->|RESTRICT| Abort["Abort Transaction with Error"]
  Policy -->|CASCADE| DeleteChildren["Recursively Delete Child Tuples"]
  Policy -->|SET NULL| NullifyChildren["Update Child Foreign Keys to NULL"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 4: Relational Model -> 4.3 Integrity Constraints

cards.front: How are Weak Entity Sets translated into relational schemas with composite primary keys and cascading foreign keys (Step 2)?
cards.back: In Step 2 of ER-to-relational mapping, for each weak entity type W with identifying strong owner entity E: create a relation R_W containing all simple and flattened composite attributes of W. Include as foreign key attributes in R_W the primary key attribute(s) of relation R_E referencing the owner. The primary key of R_W is the composite combination of the owner's primary key and the partial discriminator key of the weak entity set: PK = (PK_E, Discriminator). In SQL DDL, the foreign key constraint is declared with ON DELETE CASCADE to guarantee that child weak records are automatically pruned if the owner entity is deleted.
cards.key_takeaway: Weak entity table PK = Owner PK (as FK) + Partial Key, enforced in DDL with ON DELETE CASCADE.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  Owner["DEPARTMENT (Dept_No [PK])"]
  WeakEntity["DEPENDENT (Dep_Name [Partial], Age)"]
  Owner -->|Step 2| Rel["R_DEPENDENT (Dept_No [FK], Dep_Name, Age)"]
  Rel --> PK["Composite PK: (Dept_No, Dep_Name)"]
  Rel --> Cascade["ON DELETE CASCADE"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 5: Logical Design -> 5.3 Step 2

cards.front: What are the four architectural options (8A, 8B, 8C, 8D) for mapping Specialization/Generalization hierarchies?
cards.back: Step 8 maps EER hierarchies via four strategies: (8A) Multiple Relations for Superclass and Subclasses: Create a table for the superclass and separate tables for each subclass sharing the same PK (foreign key to superclass); valid for any constraint. (8B) Multiple Relations for Subclasses Only: Create relations only for subclasses, replicating superclass attributes into each; valid ONLY for Total + Disjoint specializations. (8C) Single Relation with One Type Attribute: Merge entire hierarchy into one table with a discriminator column and nullable subclass attributes; valid ONLY for Disjoint specializations. (8D) Single Relation with Multiple Type Flags: Merge entire hierarchy into one table with individual Boolean flags for each subclass; optimal for Overlapping specializations.
cards.key_takeaway: 8A: normalized multi-table; 8B: leaf-only tables (total disjoint); 8C: single table with discriminator (disjoint); 8D: single table with flags (overlapping).
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  Opt["EER Mapping Step 8 Options"] --> Opt8A["8A: Superclass + Subclass Relations (All Cases)"]
  Opt --> Opt8B["8B: Subclass Relations Only (Total Disjoint)"]
  Opt --> Opt8C["8C: Single Table + Type Code (Disjoint)"]
  Opt --> Opt8D["8D: Single Table + Boolean Flags (Overlapping)"]
cards.mindmap_path: DBMS UNIT - I -> Topic 5: Logical Design -> 5.8 Step 8

cards.front: What are the Five Primitive Operators of Relational Algebra and the Closure Property?
cards.back: The five fundamental primitive operators of relational algebra from which all other query operations can be derived are: (1) Selection (sigma), (2) Projection (pi), (3) Union (U), (4) Set Difference (-), and (5) Cartesian Product (x). The Closure Property guarantees that the input operands of any relational algebra operator are relations, and the output result is ALWAYS a relation; this allows relational algebra expressions to be nested and composed into arbitrarily deep algebraic query trees evaluated by cost-based optimizers.
cards.key_takeaway: The 5 primitive operators are sigma, pi, U, -, and x; Closure guarantees that every operation produces a valid relation, enabling operator nesting.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  Primitives["5 Primitive Operators"] --> S["1. Selection (sigma)"]
  Primitives --> P["2. Projection (pi)"]
  Primitives --> U["3. Union (U)"]
  Primitives --> D["4. Set Difference (-)"]
  Primitives --> C["5. Cartesian Product (x)"]
  Primitives --> Cl["Closure Property: Result is ALWAYS a relation"]
  style Cl fill:#e1f5fe,stroke:#0288d1

cards.front: What are the performance, storage, and updatability trade-offs between Virtual Views and Materialized Views?
cards.back: A View is a virtual relation defined by an underlying query: (1) Virtual Views store only the SQL definition in the data catalog; upon query execution, the view is expanded inline into the base query (view inlining), guaranteeing real-time data freshness with zero redundant storage overhead, but recalculating joins on every request. (2) Materialized Views physically compute and persist result tuples on disk; they deliver lightning-fast analytical query performance for heavy aggregations, but incur storage overhead and require Periodic or Incremental View Maintenance (IVM) to stay synchronized with base table mutations. Under ISO SQL standards, a view is updatable only if it maps 1-to-1 to a single base table without aggregations, joins, or DISTINCT.
cards.key_takeaway: Virtual views store query text with zero storage and real-time freshness; Materialized views cache computed tuples on disk for high read performance.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  Def["CREATE VIEW Sales_Summary AS ..."]
  Def -->|Virtual View| Catalog["Stores SQL Definition Only -> Re-executed on Demand"]
  Def -->|Materialized View| DiskTable["Physically Persists Rows -> Requires Refresh Policies"]

cards.front: How do DDL statements execute within ACID transactional boundaries during Schema Evolution?
cards.back: In production relational database engines (e.g., PostgreSQL), Data Definition Language (DDL) statements execute within ACID transactional boundaries: (1) The DDL interpreter acquires schema locks (such as AccessExclusiveLock) on target tables; (2) System catalog tables (such as pg_class, pg_attribute, pg_constraint) are updated transactionally; (3) If a foreign key validation or type conversion check fails, the entire DDL transaction is rolled back via Write-Ahead Log undo passes, preventing corrupted catalog states; (4) Online schema evolution techniques allow fast-path column additions and concurrent index building (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY) without locking table reads or writes.
cards.key_takeaway: Transactional DDL guarantees that schema changes (ALTER TABLE, DROP CASCADE) execute atomically under catalog transaction locks.
cards.mermaid_diagram:
graph TD
  DDL["ALTER TABLE Command"] --> Lock["Acquire Schema Lock on Table"]
  Lock --> Cat["Update System Catalog (pg_attribute)"]
  Cat --> Check{Constraint Check Pass?}
  Check -->|YES| Commit["Commit Catalog Transaction"]
  Check -->|NO| Rollback["Rollback via WAL Undo Passes"]
